findings.problem: ¡Buenas! cannot be a short form of 'buenos días' (masculine); it shortens buenas tardes / buenas noches, though it is used at any time of day.

fix.note: Casual short form of buenas tardes / buenas noches; works at any time of day, even in the morning.

findings.problem: ¿Cómo ___? with cue 'estar': 'está' (usted, or 'how is he/she') is equally valid; en/ar/vi translations do not mark informal register.
¿De dónde ___? with cue 'ser': polite 'es' is equally valid for en/ar/vi learners.
¿Dónde ___? with cue 'vivir': polite 'vive' is equally valid for en/ar/vi learners.
¿Estás ___? with cue 'seguro': 'segura' is equally valid (addressee gender unknown in en/fa/tr/vi); no other target avoids the tú/usted ambiguity (Estás/Está).
Estoy ___ (perdido): a female learner would correctly type 'perdida', which would be marked wrong.
Estoy ___ (ocupado): 'ocupada' is equally valid for a female speaker.
Estoy ___ (contento): 'contenta' is equally valid for a female speaker.
Estoy ___ (cansado): 'cansada' is equally valid for a female speaker.
Estoy ___ (enfermo): 'enferma' is equally valid for a female speaker.
Estoy ___ (aburrido): 'aburrida' is equally valid for a female speaker.
Estoy ___ (lleno): 'llena' is equally valid for a female speaker.
Soy ___ (vegetariano): 'vegetariana' is equally valid for a female speaker.
___ este, por favor (querer) with translation 'I'd like this one': 'Quisiera' is equally (arguably more) valid; targeting 'este' instead fails too, since 'esta' is valid for a feminine dish.
___ aquí, por favor (parar): tú-form 'Para' is equally valid (often used to taxi drivers; en/vi/ar translations do not mark usted).
'Vâng, làm ơn.' is a calque of 'Yes, please'; Vietnamese accepts an offer with 'cho tôi xin'.
'Làm ơn không cho đường.' is stilted; natural ordering phrase is 'Không đường nhé.' / 'Cho tôi không đường.'
¿Está ___? (abierto): with a feminine referent (la tienda, la farmacia) 'abierta' is also valid; masculine is only the neutral default.
Está ___ (cerrado): 'cerrada' is also valid for a feminine referent (la tienda).
¡Está ___! (delicioso): 'deliciosa' is also valid for a feminine dish (la comida, la sopa).

rounds.summary: The Spanish texts are correct, natural and well pitched at A1; Spain/Latin American mixing is handled well, with every chosen form understood across varieties and accurate notes, except one wrong note on ¡Buenas!. The main weakness is the cloze: gender-inflected adjectives (perdido, cansado, lleno...) and tú-form verbs whose en/ar/vi translations do not mark register admit a second valid answer. Translations are strong; only two Vietnamese lines are calqued.

newFindings.problem: '___ tarde.' (cue llegar): 'Llegué' is equally valid, especially for fa (دیر کرده‌ام, perfect), tr (Geç kaldım, past form) and vi (bị muộn rồi) learners, whose translations read as past/perfect.
'¡Qué ___!' (cue gracioso): 'graciosa' is equally valid for a feminine referent (la película, la foto); 'That's funny!' does not force masculine.
'¿Qué te ___?' (cue pasar): the fa translation چیزی شده؟ ('has something happened?') makes 'pasó' defensible for fa learners. A present-tense fa line removes it.

'Te ___.' (cue extrañar): tr 'Seni özledim' and fa 'دلم برایت تنگ شده است' are past/perfect in form, so a learner might type 'extrañé' (I missed you). Idiomatically both mean 'I miss you', so probably acceptable.

In a service situation many teachers would correct the blunt 'Quiero este' to 'Quisiera este', which is the polite register the pack rules require and matches en 'I'd like'. Ordering with quiero + por favor is common in practice, though.
'Tôi đến đây đi nghỉ.' is a bit clipped; a native would more likely write 'Tôi đến đây để đi nghỉ.'

fix.translations.vi: Tôi đến đây để đi nghỉ.
